claim: T. gondii infection of healthy individuals causes no major complications.
source: T. gondii infection of healthy individuals causes no major complications, infection can cause severe disease in immunocompromised individuals and foetuses infected in utero.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the clinical manifestations of T. gondii infection.

claim: T. gondii infection can cause severe disease in immunocompromised individuals and foetuses infected in utero.
source: T. gondii infection of healthy individuals causes no major complications, infection can cause severe disease in immunocompromised individuals and foetuses infected in utero.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the clinical manifestations of T. gondii infection.

claim: Replication in T. gondii occurs via a unique process of endodyogeny, where two daughter parasites are constructed within the mother, before elongating and budding, leading to the breakdown of the maternal parasite.
source: Replication occurs via a unique process of endodyogeny, where two daughter parasites are constructed within the mother, before elongating and budding, leading to the breakdown of the maternal parasite (Francia and Striepen, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Francia and Striepen, 2014.

claim: Remnants of the mother cell remain at the posterior end of the daughter parasites in a structure known as the residual body (RB).
source: Remnants of the mother cell remain at the posterior end of the daughter parasites in a structure known as the residual body (RB), which has a role in organizing the parasites into their characteristic rosette pattern within the PV (Muñiz-Hernández et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Muñiz-Hernández et al., 2011 and Hu et al., 2002.

claim: The residual body has a role in organizing the parasites into their characteristic rosette pattern within the PV.
source: Remnants of the mother cell remain at the posterior end of the daughter parasites in a structure known as the residual body (RB), which has a role in organizing the parasites into their characteristic rosette pattern within the PV (Muñiz-Hernández et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Muñiz-Hernández et al., 2011 and Hu et al., 2002.

claim: Membrane connections persist between the RB and the parasites until host cell lysis and parasite egress.
source: Membrane connections persist between the RB and the parasites until host cell lysis and parasite egress, presumably to allow inter-parasite communication (Muñiz-Hernández et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Muñiz-Hernández et al., 2011.

claim: Treatment with microtubule inhibitors leads to structural collapse of the parasite.
source: Previous studies focused on the role of microtubules during parasite replication, since treatment with microtubule inhibitors leads to structural collapse of the parasite, while actin-modulating drugs are thought to cause only slight defects in replication (Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: Actin-modulating drugs are thought to cause only slight defects in replication.
source: Previous studies focused on the role of microtubules during parasite replication, since treatment with microtubule inhibitors leads to structural collapse of the parasite, while actin-modulating drugs are thought to cause only slight defects in replication (Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: Parasite actin has a crucial role during host cell invasion and egress.
source: In contrast, research on parasite actin focused on its crucial role during host cell invasion and egress (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996.

claim: Recent studies have implicated actin and myosins in apicoplast division.
source: However, recent studies have also implicated actin and myosins in intracellular processes including apicoplast division (Egarter et al., 2014; Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013), secretory organelle (dense granule) transport (Heaslip et al., 2016) and parasite replication (Haase et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Egarter et al., 2014; Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013.

claim: Recent studies have implicated actin and myosins in secretory organelle (dense granule) transport.
source: However, recent studies have also implicated actin and myosins in intracellular processes including apicoplast division (Egarter et al., 2014; Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013), secretory organelle (dense granule) transport (Heaslip et al., 2016) and parasite replication (Haase et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Heaslip et al., 2016.

claim: Recent studies have implicated actin and myosins in parasite replication.
source: However, recent studies have also implicated actin and myosins in intracellular processes including apicoplast division (Egarter et al., 2014; Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013), secretory organelle (dense granule) transport (Heaslip et al., 2016) and parasite replication (Haase et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Haase et al., 2015.

claim: T. gondii actin is encoded by a single gene, act1.
source: T. gondii actin is encoded by a single gene, act1 and has only ~80% sequence identity with mammalian actin isoforms but shares 93% similarity with Plasmodium ACT1 (Dobrowolski et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dobrowolski et al., 1997.

claim: T. gondii actin has only ~80% sequence identity with mammalian actin isoforms.
source: T. gondii actin is encoded by a single gene, act1 and has only ~80% sequence identity with mammalian actin isoforms but shares 93% similarity with Plasmodium ACT1 (Dobrowolski et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dobrowolski et al., 1997.

claim: T. gondii actin shares 93% similarity with Plasmodium ACT1.
source: T. gondii actin is encoded by a single gene, act1 and has only ~80% sequence identity with mammalian actin isoforms but shares 93% similarity with Plasmodium ACT1 (Dobrowolski et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dobrowolski et al., 1997.

claim: Apicomplexan ACT1 is clearly essential.
source: Apicomplexan ACT1 is clearly essential, and compared to its counterparts in higher eukaryotes is believed to be intrinsically unstable, resulting in the formation of only short filaments (Skillman et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Skillman et al., 2011.

claim: Apicomplexan ACT1 is believed to be intrinsically unstable, resulting in the formation of only short filaments.
source: Apicomplexan ACT1 is clearly essential, and compared to its counterparts in higher eukaryotes is believed to be intrinsically unstable, resulting in the formation of only short filaments (Skillman et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Skillman et al., 2011.

claim: Biochemical assays indicate that 97% of the parasites actin is present in the globular form.
source: Biochemical assays indicate that 97% of the parasites actin is present in the globular form (Dobrowolski et al., 1997; Skillman et al., 2011; Wetzel et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dobrowolski et al., 1997; Skillman et al., 2011; Wetzel et al., 2003.

claim: It has been proposed that apicomplexan actin polymerizes in a highly unusual, isodesmic manner.
source: It has been proposed that apicomplexan actin is unique amongst actins as it polymerizes in a highly unusual, isodesmic manner (Skillman et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Skillman et al., 2013.

claim: Formins and other actin nucleating proteins have been shown to have essential roles in Toxoplasma and Plasmodium.
source: Puzzlingly, formins and other actin nucleating proteins have been shown to have essential roles in Toxoplasma and Plasmodium, begging the question of their function if they are not required to initiate actin polymerisation or accelerate filament elongation (Baum et al., 2008; Jacot et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Baum et al., 2008; Jacot et al., 2013.

claim: Heterologously expressed apicomplexan actin is incorrectly folded.
source: A recent study suggested that the polymerization process of apicomplexan actin needs to be reinvestigated, as heterologously expressed apicomplexan actin, the basis for many of the previous studies, is incorrectly folded (Olshina et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Olshina et al., 2016.

claim: Conditional deletion of act1 in T. gondii results in complete abrogation of known actin functions, long before G-actin levels are fully depleted.
source: Furthermore, it was demonstrated that conditional deletion of act1 in T. gondii results in complete abrogation of known actin functions, long before G-actin levels are fully depleted, suggesting that in vivo the formation of F-actin depends on a critical monomer concentration (Whitelaw et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claim: In vivo the formation of F-actin depends on a critical monomer concentration.
source: Furthermore, it was demonstrated that conditional deletion of act1 in T. gondii results in complete abrogation of known actin functions, long before G-actin levels are fully depleted, suggesting that in vivo the formation of F-actin depends on a critical monomer concentration (Whitelaw et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Whitelaw et al., 2017 and is presented as a suggestion based on the cited work.

claim: Imaging studies on different life cycle stages of Plasmodium falciparum demonstrated the formation of an extensive F-actin cytoskeleton in both gametocytes and ookinetes.
source: Furthermore, imaging studies on different life cycle stages of the apicomplexan parasite, Plasmodium falciparum, demonstrated the formation of an extensive F-actin cytoskeleton in both gametocytes and ookinetes (Hliscs et al., 2015; Siden-Kiamos et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hliscs et al., 2015; Siden-Kiamos et al., 2012.

claim: Using 3D-SIM it was demonstrated in gametocytes that actin filaments appear to be organized in the cytoplasm, below the Inner Membrane Complex (IMC) of the parasite.
source: Using 3D-SIM it was demonstrated in gametocytes that these filaments appear to be organized in the cytoplasm, below the Inner Membrane Complex (IMC; a specialised structure found in apicomplexans that consists of membranous vesicles and structural components located just beneath the plasma membrane) of the parasite rather than between the IMC and the plasma membrane (Hliscs et al., 2015), where it is thought to power parasite gliding motility (Meissner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hliscs et al., 2015.

claim: act1 cKO parasites lack a residual body.
source: We demonstrate that act1 cKO parasites lack a residual body and grow in an asynchronous and disorganized manner within the PV.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: act1 cKO parasites grow in an asynchronous and disorganized manner within the PV.
source: We demonstrate that act1 cKO parasites lack a residual body and grow in an asynchronous and disorganized manner within the PV.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Conventional actin labelling techniques such as Life-Act, Phalloidin and SiR-Act do not allow detection of F-actin within the parasites.
source: Previous attempts to visualise F-actin within the parasites have largely been unsuccessful, since conventional actin labelling techniques such as Life-Act, Phalloidin and SiR-Act do not allow detection of F-actin within the parasites.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge based on previous attempts.

claim: GFP-actin shows a high signal to noise ratio in parasites causing the inability to differentiate actin filaments from the monomeric form.
source: GFP-actin shows a high signal to noise ratio in parasites causing the inability to differentiate actin filaments from the monomeric form Angrisano et al. (2012a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Angrisano et al. (2012a).

claim: Actin-chromobody is a single chain anti-actin camel antibody that has been successfully employed in diverse eukaryotes, including plants and animal cells.
source: Thus we sought a new approach to image F-actin in intracellular parasites by expressing actin-chromobody, a single chain anti-actin camel antibody that has been successfully employed in diverse eukaryotes, including plants (Rocchetti et al., 2014) and animal cells (Plessner et al., 2015; Panza et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rocchetti et al., 2014; Plessner et al., 2015; Panza et al., 2015.

claim: Chromobodies (Cb) have several advantages compared to other actin probes, such as lower toxicity, less influence on F-actin dynamics and a high signal to noise ratio.
source: Chromobodies (Cb) were found to have several advantages compared to other actin probes, such as lower toxicity, less influence on F-actin dynamics and a high signal to noise ratio (Panza et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Panza et al., 2015.

claim: Using the chromobody probe, extensive F-actin networks were observed in the RB and F-actin-containing membranous tubules linking parasites within a vacuole.
source: Using this probe, we were able to visualise filamentous actin in live parasites. While some filamentous structures were seen within the parasite cytosol as expected, we were surprised to observe extensive F-actin networks in the RB and F-actin-containing membranous tubules linking parasites within a vacuole.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The F-actin-containing tubules appear to be involved in the transport of material between parasites and recycling of the mother IMC at the end of the replication cycle.
source: These tubules appear to be involved in the transport of material between parasites and recycling of the mother IMC at the end of the replication cycle.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Initially intracellular act1 cKO parasites replicate at comparable rate to wild-type parasites.
source: Although initially intracellular act1 cKO parasites replicate at comparable rate to wild-type parasites (Egarter et al., 2014), they grew asynchronously and appeared disorganised, without the characteristic rosette organization of parasites in the parasitophorous vacuole (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Egarter et al., 2014.

claim: act1 cKO parasites replicate normally up to the 4 cell stage, but later divisions are not tightly synchronised.
source: While parasites replicate normally up to the 4 cell stage, later divisions are not tightly synchronised (Figure 1A), meaning that within the same PV parasites can be identified that are at different stages of endodyogeny (Figure 1B, arrow).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: In wild-type (RH) T. gondii a membranous network connects parasites at their posterior pole.
source: Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of intracellular parasites, we observed that in wild-type (RH) T. gondii a membranous network connects parasites at their posterior pole whereas no obvious connections between individual parasites were observed in the act1 cKO (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by SEM data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No obvious connections between individual parasites were observed in the act1 cKO.
source: Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of intracellular parasites, we observed that in wild-type (RH) T. gondii a membranous network connects parasites at their posterior pole whereas no obvious connections between individual parasites were observed in the act1 cKO (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by SEM data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Imaging of extracellular parasites by SEM and immunofluorescence showed aberrant morphology at the posterior pole in the act1 cKO parasites, which appears generally flattened.
source: In addition, imaging of extracellular parasites by SEM and immunofluorescence showed aberrant morphology at the posterior pole in the act1 cKO parasites, which appears generally flattened (Figure 1C, arrow).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by SEM and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Actin is involved in the formation of the RB, the organization of parasites within the PV and the intravacuolar network.
source: Together, these data suggest a role of actin in the formation of the RB, the organization of parasites within the PV and the intravacuolar network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Asynchronous replication of parasites within the PV may indicate a loss of signalling between individual parasites.
source: Furthermore, asynchronous replication of parasites within the PV may indicate a loss of signalling between individual parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed asynchronous replication.

claim: The RB has been predicted to be involved in the transfer of material between parasites within a vacuole.
source: Based on electron microscopy evidence, the RB has been predicted to be involved in the transfer of material between parasites within a vacuole (Muñiz-Hernández et al., 2011) although this has not been previously demonstrated.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Muñiz-Hernández et al., 2011.

claim: The fluorescence signal recovered rapidly in wt parasites (~30 s) after FRAP.
source: To investigate this hypothesis and the role of actin in this process, we infected host cells with wt or act1 cKO parasites expressing GFP and bleached individual parasites within the PV before measuring the time of fluorescence recovery (Videos 1 and 2; Figure 2A). While the fluorescence signal recovered rapidly in wt parasites (~30 s), no fluorescence recovery could be observed in parasites depleted of actin, indicating a defect in material transfer (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2A and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: No fluorescence recovery could be observed in parasites depleted of actin after FRAP, indicating a defect in material transfer.
source: To investigate this hypothesis and the role of actin in this process, we infected host cells with wt or act1 cKO parasites expressing GFP and bleached individual parasites within the PV before measuring the time of fluorescence recovery (Videos 1 and 2; Figure 2A). While the fluorescence signal recovered rapidly in wt parasites (~30 s), no fluorescence recovery could be observed in parasites depleted of actin, indicating a defect in material transfer (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2A and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Individual parasites remain connected via the intravacuolar network and can exchange cytoplasmic material.
source: From this experiment, we concluded that individual parasites remain connected via the intravacuolar network and can exchange cytoplasmic material.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP experiments.

claim: The connections between parasites appear to be actin dependent.
source: Furthermore, these connections appear to be actin dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP experiments comparing wt and act1 cKO parasites.

claim: Vesicles positive for GAPM1a-YFP were seen to be transported in wt parasites.
source: To determine if vesicular as well as cytoplasmic material could be transferred between parasites, we performed time-lapse analysis of the integral membrane protein GAPM1a-YFP (Figure 2B) and identified vesicles moving in a directed manner, demonstrating that vesicular transport occurs outside of the parasite (Figure 2B, Video 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Video 3.

claim: Vesicular transport occurs outside of the parasite.
source: To determine if vesicular as well as cytoplasmic material could be transferred between parasites, we performed time-lapse analysis of the integral membrane protein GAPM1a-YFP (Figure 2B) and identified vesicles moving in a directed manner, demonstrating that vesicular transport occurs outside of the parasite (Figure 2B, Video 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Video 3.

claim: Digital tracking of vesicles suggested a directional movement along a tubular or filamentous structure.
source: Of note, digital tracking of vesicles suggested a directional movement along a tubular or filamentous structure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the digital tracking of vesicles.

claim: Individual parasites within a vacuole remain connected via a network, possibly through the RB that is required to transfer both cytoplasmic and membrane bound material between individual parasites.
source: In summary, these data indicate that individual parasites within a vacuole remain connected via a network, possibly through the RB that is required to transfer both cytoplasmic and membrane bound material between individual parasites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Parasite actin is required for the formation and/or maintenance of this interconnecting network.
source: We hypothesize that parasite actin is required for the formation and/or maintenance of this interconnecting network.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claim: Upon transient expression of Cb fusion proteins, individual parasites within the PV remain connected by a filamentous actin network which stretches throughout the RB and parasitophorous vacuole.
source: Upon transient expression of these proteins, we obtained identical staining of filamentous structures within the parasites. Cb was also localised somewhat diffusely in the parasite cytosol, probably corresponding to unbound Cb in the cytosol as the protein was expressed at a high level (Figure 3A). Strikingly, individual parasites within the PV remain connected by a filamentous actin network which stretches throughout the RB and parasitophorous vacuole and can be seen to enter the posterior pole of individual parasites (Figure 3A, arrow).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of intracellular parasites appeared healthy with no apparent morphological changes during transient expressions of the Cb fusion proteins, indicating that expression of Cb-proteins is well tolerated by the parasite.
source: During transient expressions of the fusion proteins, the majority of intracellular parasites appeared healthy with no apparent morphological changes, indicating that expression of Cb-proteins is well tolerated by the parasite.
evidence: This is an observation from the transient expression experiments.

claim: Strong expression of Cb-Halo leads to an almost complete block of dense granule motility.
source: Parasites stably expressing SAG1-ΔGPI-GFP (to label the dense granules) were transiently transfected with Cb-Halo and dense granule motility was analysed and correlated to mean fluorescent intensity of Cb-Halo within the parasite (Video 4; Figure 3C). Strong expression of Cb-Halo leads to an almost complete block of dense granule motility, however, weaker expression levels are well tolerated with no significant change in either dense granule run frequency (Figure 3C) or run length compared to controls (935 ± 39 nm vs 1013 ± 53 nm for control and Cb-Halo, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by dense granule motility data shown in Figure 3C and Video 4.

claim: Weaker expression levels of Cb-Halo are well tolerated with no significant change in either dense granule run frequency or run length compared to controls.
source: Parasites stably expressing SAG1-ΔGPI-GFP (to label the dense granules) were transiently transfected with Cb-Halo and dense granule motility was analysed and correlated to mean fluorescent intensity of Cb-Halo within the parasite (Video 4; Figure 3C). Strong expression of Cb-Halo leads to an almost complete block of dense granule motility, however, weaker expression levels are well tolerated with no significant change in either dense granule run frequency (Figure 3C) or run length compared to controls (935 ± 39 nm vs 1013 ± 53 nm for control and Cb-Halo, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by dense granule motility data shown in Figure 3C and Video 4.

claim: Expression of Cb is well tolerated by the parasite indicating that it does not significantly adversely affect normal actin functions within the cell.
source: In summary, expression of Cb is well tolerated by the parasite indicating that it does not significantly adversely affect normal actin functions within the cell, in agreement to data obtained in other cellular systems (Belin et al., 2014; Panza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by citations to Belin et al., 2014; Panza et al., 2015.

claim: Parasite growth, invasion, replication and egress rates are indistinguishable from wt parasites in stable parasite lines expressing either Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald.
source: As transient transfection resulted in a heterologous population of parasites expressing Cb at varying levels, which may be deleterious for the parasites, we generated stable parasite lines expressing either Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald and confirmed that parasite growth, invasion, replication and egress rates are indistinguishable from wt parasites (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4A-E.

claim: The rate of overall motility is slightly increased (p<0.05) upon expression of Cb.
source: We found that the rate of overall motility is slightly increased (p<0.05) upon expression of Cb (Figure 4F), indicating an influence of Cb expression on actin dynamics.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Average trajectory lengths are identical in wt and Cb expressing parasites.
source: Intriguingly, average trajectory lengths are identical in wt and Cb expressing parasites (Figure 4G), while average gliding speed is reduced (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Average gliding speed is reduced in Cb expressing parasites.
source: Intriguingly, average trajectory lengths are identical in wt and Cb expressing parasites (Figure 4G), while average gliding speed is reduced (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Parasites penetrate the host cell within 30 s irrespective of Cb expression.
source: We also analysed average invasion speeds and confirmed that parasites penetrate the host cell within 30 s irrespective of Cb expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Time lapse imaging of Cb-Emerald demonstrated a highly dynamic behaviour of F-actin within the cytosol.
source: Furthermore, time lapse imaging of Cb-Emerald demonstrated a highly dynamic behaviour of F-actin within the cytosol (Video 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 5.

claim: The expression of this actin binding protein has no or modest effects on established actin-dependent processes in T. gondii.
source: Together these data demonstrate that, similar to the situation in other eukaryotes, the expression of this actin binding protein has no or modest effects on established actin-dependent processes in T. gondii.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recombinant Cb bound to chicken skeletal actin with Kd of 5 ± 1 µM.
source: Recombinant Cb with a C-terminal 6-His tag (rCb) was expressed and purified from bacteria (Figure 5A,B). rCb bound to chicken skeletal actin with Kd of 5 ± 1 µM (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only a small proportion of actin was precipitated in co-immunoprecipitation experiments, which corresponds well with published data suggesting that only ~2% of total parasite actin can be found in its filamentous form in extracellular parasites.
source: To confirm that Cb-Halo binds specifically to Toxoplasma F-actin when expressed in the parasite, we co-immunoprecipitated actin from extracellular parasites using an anti-Halo antibody (Figure 5C). As expected, only a small proportion of actin was precipitated, which corresponds well with published data suggesting that only ~2% of total parasite actin can be found in its filamentous form in extracellular parasites (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1997).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C and a citation to Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1997.

claim: Mass-spectrometric analysis of the immunoprecipitation confirmed that Cb-Halo specifically precipitated parasite actin.
source: Importantly, mass-spectrometric analysis of the immunoprecipitation confirmed that Cb-Halo specifically precipitated parasite actin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: No host cell actin, actin related or actin-like proteins could be identified in the immunoprecipitation.
source: Although additional, potential F-actin binding proteins were detected, no host cell actin, actin related or actin-like proteins could be identified (not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: F-actin is barely detectable in extracellular parasites, indicating that it is primarily found in globular form.
source: To assess if expression of Cb stabilises F-actin in parasites, we compared the amount of pelletable actin in parasites expressing Cb and wt parasites (Figure 5D). We confirmed that in both cases F-actin is barely detectable in extracellular parasites, indicating that it is primarily found in globular form.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Treatment of parasites with Jas allowed detection of significant amount of F-actin in the pellet.
source: Treatment of parasites with Jas allowed detection of significant amount of F-actin in the pellet.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sedimentation assay data.

claim: No significant difference could be observed between control parasites and parasites expressing Cb in the amount of pelletable actin.
source: Of note, no significant difference could be observed between control parasites and parasites expressing Cb.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sedimentation assay data.

claim: Expression of Cb in parasites allows detection of F-actin and that Cb expression has only minor effects on F-actin dynamics.
source: Together, these data confirm that expression of Cb in parasites allows detection of F-actin and that Cb expression has only minor effects on F-actin dynamics, as previously shown in other eukaryotes (Panza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by a citation to Panza et al., 2015.

claim: Treatment of intracellular parasites with Cyt-D led to the disintegration of the inter-parasite connections with only punctate spots remaining.
source: Using actin-modulating drugs, the actin cytoskeleton was either depolymerized with Cytochalasin D (Cyt-D) or stabilized with Jasplakinolide (Jas). Treatment of intracellular parasites with Cyt-D led to the disintegration of the inter-parasite connections with only punctate spots remaining, which were also identified with anti-actin antibody (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Treatment with Jas led to the stabilisation of F-actin and intra-parasite connections were easily detectable with either Cb or an anti-actin antibody.
source: In contrast, treatment with Jas led to the stabilisation of F-actin and intra-parasite connections were easily detectable with either Cb or an anti-actin antibody (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In Jas-treated PVs, there is an increase in average and maximum filament size, together with a decrease in total number of short filaments.
source: Using default settings of the Ridge Detector plugin (Steger, 1998) we determined the apparent number, maximum length and average filament size of PVs treated with Jas, Cyt-D or untreated PVs (control) (Figure 6A right panel). In Jas-treated PVs, and in contrast to Cyt-D treated PVs, there is an increase in average and maximum filament size, together with a decrease in total number of short filaments supporting the stabilisation and depolymerisation of Cb-Halo detected filaments in the presence of Jas and Cyt-D respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cb-Halo is specifically labelling F-actin filaments and that Cb binding to actin does not prevent depolymerisation caused by Cyt-D.
source: Overall, these results support that filaments detected with Cb-Halo behave as typical actin filaments in the presence of actin regulatory drugs. This supports the evidence that Cb-Halo is specifically labelling F-actin filaments and that Cb binding to actin does not prevent depolymerisation caused by Cyt-D.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with actin-modulating drugs.

claim: As early as 24 hr after excision of the act1 gene, the filamentous network collapsed, leaving punctate actin spots visible only in the RBs.
source: To confirm that parasite F-actin corresponds to Cb-positive structures, we expressed Cb-Halo in act1 cKO cells. Using these parasites, we found that as early as 24 hr after excision of the act1 gene, the filamentous network collapsed, leaving punctate actin spots visible only in the RBs (similar to vacuoles treated with Cyt-D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: By 48 hr onwards after excision of act1, no F-actin structures could be observed and Cb-Halo was completely cytosolic.
source: By 48 hr onwards, no F-actin structures could be observed and Cb-Halo was completely cytosolic, as expected due to cytosolic expression of this reagent (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The loss of filaments within the act1 cKO over-time follows the down-regulation of ACT1 in act1 cKO, indicating a polymerisation mechanism similar to eukaryotic actins.
source: The loss of filaments within the act1 cKO over-time follows the down-regulation of ACT1 in act1 cKO, indicating a polymerisation mechanism similar to eukaryotic actins (Whitelaw et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by a citation to Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claim: Latrunculin A treatment for 3 hr led to complete disruption of host cell F-actin, while the parasite F-actin network remained unaffected.
source: To exclude a role of host cell actin in the formation of the inter-parasite connections, we treated infected host cells with the actin-disrupting drug latrunculin A, which specifically inhibits polymerization of host cell, but not parasite, actin (Hegge et al., 2010; Whitelaw et al., 2017). We found that latrunculin A treatment for 3 hr led to complete disruption of host cell F-actin (visualised using Phalloidin488), while the parasite F-actin network remained unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C and citations to Hegge et al., 2010; Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claim: Cb-positive filamentous structures were not derived from host cell actin.
source: This confirms that Cb-positive filamentous structures were not derived from host cell actin (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the latrunculin A treatment experiment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In absence of anhydrotetracycline (ATc) - when ADF is expressed - parasite F-actin shows a highly dynamic behaviour similar to wt parasites.
source: When we expressed Cb-Emerald in adf cKD to compare actin dynamics, we found that in absence of anhydrotetracycline (ATc) - when ADF is expressed - parasite F-actin shows a highly dynamic behaviour similar to wt parasites (Figure 6D, compare Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6D and Videos 6 and 7.

claim: Incubation of parasites with ATc for 96 hr leads to depletion of ADF and consequently F-actin dynamics is significantly diminished.
source: In stark contrast, incubation of parasites with ATc for 96 hr leads to depletion of ADF and consequently F-actin dynamics is significantly diminished.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data.

claim: Upon depletion of ADF, F-actin filaments accumulate at the posterior and to a lesser extent at the apical pole of the parasites.
source: Under these conditions F-actin filaments accumulate at the posterior and to a lesser extent at the apical pole of the parasites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data.

claim: Upon depletion of ADF, no dynamic behaviour can be detected and no filaments can be detected within the cytosol of the parasites.
source: However, no dynamic behaviour can be detected and no filaments can be detected within the cytosol of the parasites (Figure 6D (red arrows), Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6D and Videos 6 and 7.

claim: In non-replicating parasites F-actin forms an extended, continuous filamentous network through the RB, connecting the parasites.
source: Using time-lapse analysis, we found that in non-replicating parasites F-actin forms an extended, continuous filamentous network through the RB, connecting the parasites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claim: During parasite replication, the F-actin network collapses and F-actin retreats to the RB before the network reform again, extending throughout the PV.
source: During parasite replication, this network collapses and F-actin retreats to the RB (asterisks) before the network reform again, extending throughout the PV (Figure 7A, Video 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 7A and Video 8.

claim: The F-actin filaments appear relatively static in resting parasites and do not show much reorientation/movement within 8 hr.
source: Note that these filaments appear relatively static in resting parasites and do not show much reorientation/movement within 8 hr.
evidence: This is an observation from the time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Once parasites start to replicate within the PV, the connections disintegrate and F-actin appears to be restricted to the RB.
source: However, once parasites start to replicate within the PV, the connections disintegrate and F-actin appears to be restricted to the RB (Figures 7A and 8A, Videos 8 and 12).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figures 7A and 8A, Videos 8 and 12.

claim: The F-actin network collapses rapidly, between 10 and 60 s after Ca2+-Ionophore addition.
source: When we triggered a calcium signalling cascade using Ca2+-Ionophore (Black et al., 2000), the F-actin network collapsed rapidly, between 10 and 60 s after Ca2+-Ionophore addition (Figure 7B, Video 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 7B and Video 9, and a citation to Black et al., 2000.

claim: Collapse of the network preceded the initiation of motility and egress from the host cell.
source: Collapse of the network preceded the initiation of motility and egress from the host cell (Figure 7B, arrow head; Video 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 7B and Video 9.

claim: As the parasites begin to move away from the lysed host cell, F-actin can be detected at the rear of the parasites.
source: As the parasites begin to move away from the lysed host cell, F-actin can be detected at the rear of the parasites (Figure 7B, inset) and residual filamentous actin is still seen within the RB.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Extracellular F-actin filaments reside within membranous tubules of 50–60 nm in diameter.
source: To investigate the presence of F-actin within this network, we performed correlative light-electron microscopy (CLEM). The network within a vacuole was imaged using 3D structural illumination super-resolution microscopy (3D-SIM) (Figure 7C). Thin sections of the same network were then imaged with transmission electron microscopy (squares). This demonstrated that extracellular F-actin filaments reside within membranous tubules of 50–60 nm in diameter.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Within these tubules, several ~5 nm thick filaments extending over 100 nm in length were observed.
source: Within these tubules, several ~5 nm thick filaments (arrows) extending over 100 nm in length were observed (highlighted in magenta).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The membranous network consists of bundles of actin filaments bound within a membranous network, which connects individual parasites within the PV.
source: Taken together these results confirm the presence of bundles of actin filaments bound within a membranous network, which connects individual parasites within the PV.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CLEM data.

claim: F-actin dynamics within the parasite cytosol is very fast and recovery rates very rapid, within 20 s.
source: Given that the inter-parasite tubules are reorganized during both replication and egress, we investigated the dynamic behaviour of F-actin within individual tubules using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP). While F-actin dynamics within the parasite cytosol is very fast (Video 10) and recovery rates very rapid, within 20 s (Figure 7D), we found that F-actin within the tubular network is much more stable and fluorescence labelling of these structures took more than 60 s to fully recover (Video 11).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7D and Video 10.

claim: F-actin within the tubular network is much more stable and fluorescence labelling of these structures took more than 60 s to fully recover.
source: Given that the inter-parasite tubules are reorganized during both replication and egress, we investigated the dynamic behaviour of F-actin within individual tubules using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP). While F-actin dynamics within the parasite cytosol is very fast (Video 10) and recovery rates very rapid, within 20 s (Figure 7D), we found that F-actin within the tubular network is much more stable and fluorescence labelling of these structures took more than 60 s to fully recover (Video 11).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7D and Video 11.

claim: There is the presence of highly dynamic, intracellular F-actin and a stable F-actin containing filamentous network.
source: This demonstrates the presence of highly dynamic, intracellular F-actin and a stable F-actin containing filamentous network (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: During early stages of daughter cell formation, F-actin was found in the RB linking the two parasites at their posterior end.
source: Finally, given that act1 cKO parasites divided asynchronously we wanted to readdress the role of actin in parasite replication. We generated parasites co-expressing GAPM1a-YFP and Cb-Halo and performed live imaging (Figure 8A, Video 12). During early stages of daughter cell formation, F-actin was found in the RB linking the two parasites at their posterior end (Figure 8A; 1.24–2.36 hr).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A and Video 12.

claim: At the earliest stages of daughter cell construction, F-actin accumulated at the elongating IMC.
source: At the earliest stages of daughter cell construction, F-actin accumulated at the elongating IMC (Figure 8A: 1.36–2.36 hr) and further concentrated towards the posterior end of the mother cells, where it colocalized with the mother IMC (Figure 8A, 3.00–3.24 hr).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: As the daughters begin to bud from the maternal cell, the IMC of the mother disintegrates and appears to be transported towards the daughter cells.
source: As the daughters begin to bud from the maternal cell, the IMC of the mother disintegrates and appears to be transported towards the daughter cells (Figure 8A, Arrows, 3.24–3.48 hr).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: At the end of replication, the now mature parasites remain connected through F-actin structures.
source: At the end of replication, the now mature parasites remain connected through F-actin structures (Figure 8A, 4.00–5.12 hr).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: GAPM1a-YFP vesicles moved outside the parasite along filamentous tubules.
source: Given that GAPM1a-YFP positive vesicles appear to be transported between individual parasites within a PV or between parasites and the residual body (Figures 2B and 8A) we wished to further define the role the filamentous network plays in this process. We imaged Cb-Halo and GAPM1a-YFP co-expressing parasites and tracked the motion of vesicles within the residual body. GAPM1a-YFP vesicles moved outside the parasite along filamentous tubules (Figure 8B), demonstrating vesicular transport within the residual body, as also shown for wt parasites (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Transport of vesicles was dependent on F-actin, as incubation of parasites with Cyt-D significantly abrogated vesicular transport.
source: Importantly, transport of vesicles was dependent on F-actin, as incubation of parasites with Cyt-D significantly abrogated vesicular transport (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Individual parasites remain connected via an F-actin containing network that is required to transfer material in an active, F-actin dependent process.
source: In summary, these data demonstrate that individual parasites remain connected via an F-actin containing network that is required to transfer material in an active, F-actin dependent process (Video 13).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Studies on Toxoplasma actin performed in the 90's suggested that apicomplexan actin is highly divergent and incapable of forming stable filaments.
source: Studies on Toxoplasma actin performed in the 90's suggested that apicomplexan actin is highly divergent and incapable of forming stable filaments (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1997; Dobrowolski et al., 1997; Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1997; Dobrowolski et al., 1997; Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996.

claim: Polymerization kinetics of heterologously expressed apicomplexan actin showed that it polymerized in an unusual isodesmic process, in contrast to conventional eukaryotic actin.
source: Since then, polymerization kinetics of heterologously expressed apicomplexan actin showed that it polymerized in an unusual isodesmic process, in contrast to conventional eukaryotic actin (Skillman et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Skillman et al., 2013.

claim: These findings have been recently questioned, as heterologously expressed apicomplexan actin was shown to be misfolded.
source: These findings have been recently questioned, as heterologously expressed apicomplexan actin was shown to be misfolded (Olshina et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Olshina et al., 2016.

claim: A number of recent genetic studies have demonstrated important functions of parasite actin during intracellular development, including maintenance of the apicoplast.
source: In parallel, a number of recent genetic studies have demonstrated important functions of parasite actin during intracellular development, including maintenance of the apicoplast (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014), daughter cell replication (Haase et al., 2015) and motility of secretory organelles (Heaslip et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014.

claim: A number of recent genetic studies have demonstrated important functions of parasite actin during intracellular development, including daughter cell replication.
source: In parallel, a number of recent genetic studies have demonstrated important functions of parasite actin during intracellular development, including maintenance of the apicoplast (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014), daughter cell replication (Haase et al., 2015) and motility of secretory organelles (Heaslip et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Haase et al., 2015.

claim: A number of recent genetic studies have demonstrated important functions of parasite actin during intracellular development, including motility of secretory organelles.
source: In parallel, a number of recent genetic studies have demonstrated important functions of parasite actin during intracellular development, including maintenance of the apicoplast (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014), daughter cell replication (Haase et al., 2015) and motility of secretory organelles (Heaslip et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Heaslip et al., 2016.

claim: There are 11 putative myosin motors within the parasite, driving diverse cellular processes from cell division to motility, which require actin filaments to function.
source: Furthermore, there are 11 putative myosin motors within the parasite (Foth et al., 2006), driving diverse cellular processes from cell division to motility, which require actin filaments to function.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Foth et al., 2006.

claim: Parasite actin does not bind phalloidin.
source: Parasite actin does not bind phalloidin, the gold standard reagent in other eukaryotic systems (Skillman et al., 2011) and, attempts to use genetically encoded actin sensors, such a LifeAct (Riedl et al., 2008) or Utrophin-CH (Burkel et al., 2007) have failed thus far (our and others unpublished data).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Skillman et al., 2011.

claim: Attempts to use genetically encoded actin sensors, such a LifeAct or Utrophin-CH have failed thus far.
source: Parasite actin does not bind phalloidin, the gold standard reagent in other eukaryotic systems (Skillman et al., 2011) and, attempts to use genetically encoded actin sensors, such a LifeAct (Riedl et al., 2008) or Utrophin-CH (Burkel et al., 2007) have failed thus far (our and others unpublished data).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Riedl et al., 2008 and Burkel et al., 2007, and unpublished data.

claim: Using a novel tool based on camelid nanobodies, Chromobody, F-actin has been visualized in T. gondii for the first time in live parasites.
source: Using a novel tool based on camelid nanobodies, Chromobody, we have visualized F-actin in T. gondii for the first time in live parasites and demonstrated it has important and previously unforeseen roles during the intracellular development of the parasite.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: F-actin has important and previously unforeseen roles during the intracellular development of the parasite.
source: Using a novel tool based on camelid nanobodies, Chromobody, we have visualized F-actin in T. gondii for the first time in live parasites and demonstrated it has important and previously unforeseen roles during the intracellular development of the parasite.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: A relatively stable F-actin network was clearly visible that linked individual parasites within the vacuole.
source: While individual actin filament kinetics could not be easily defined, due to their highly dynamic nature within the parasite cytosol (Videos 5–7), a relatively stable F-actin network was clearly visible that linked individual parasites within the vacuole.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Videos 5-7.

claim: Chromobodies have been used successfully in diverse eukaryotes to analyse actin dynamics and appear to have less toxicity than other F-actin sensors.
source: Chromobodies have been used successfully in diverse eukaryotes to analyse actin dynamics (Panza et al., 2015; Plessner et al., 2015; Rocchetti et al., 2014) and appear to have less toxicity than other F-actin sensors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Panza et al., 2015; Plessner et al., 2015; Rocchetti et al., 2014.

claim: High levels of transiently expressed Cb inhibited dense granule motility, likely by stabilizing F-actin.
source: Indeed, high levels of transiently expressed Cb inhibited dense granule motility, likely by stabilizing F-actin (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Upon stable expression of Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald, no effect on the actin-dependent processes of invasion, replication and egress were observed.
source: However, upon stable expression of Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald, no effect on the actin-dependent processes of invasion, replication and egress were observed, while only small alterations in dense granule movement and parasite motility were detectable (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Only small alterations in dense granule movement and parasite motility were detectable upon stable expression of Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald.
source: However, upon stable expression of Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald, no effect on the actin-dependent processes of invasion, replication and egress were observed, while only small alterations in dense granule movement and parasite motility were detectable (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The total amount of F-actin in the parasite does not change upon expression of Cb.
source: Additionally, we demonstrated that the total amount of F-actin in the parasite does not change upon expression of Cb (Figure 5), indicating that while actin dynamics may be modulated, the overall polymerization state of actin does not change.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: While actin dynamics may be modulated by Cb expression, the overall polymerization state of actin does not change.
source: Additionally, we demonstrated that the total amount of F-actin in the parasite does not change upon expression of Cb (Figure 5), indicating that while actin dynamics may be modulated, the overall polymerization state of actin does not change.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Parasite actin remains susceptible to depolymerising and stabilizing agents Cyt-D and Jas.
source: We show that parasite actin remains susceptible to depolymerising and stabilizing agents Cyt-D and Jas.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The localization of Cb to filamentous structures in the residual body and inter-parasite network critically depends on the presence of actin.
source: Moreover, the localization of Cb to filamentous structures in the residual body and inter-parasite network critically depends on the presence of actin (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Genetically encoded Cb-Halo and Cb-Emerald does not significantly alter actin dynamics within the parasite and so is an appropriate and robust tool for examining F-actin in this system.
source: These data confirm that genetically encoded Cb-Halo and Cb-Emerald does not significantly alter actin dynamics within the parasite and so is an appropriate and robust tool for examining F-actin in this system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of actin in the RB and inter-parasite tubules has not previously been observed or predicted.
source: The presence of actin in the RB and inter-parasite tubules has not previously been observed or predicted, and so we sought to independently verify that this localization was not an artefact of Cb expression.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge based on the literature.

claim: Labelling parasites with α-actin that preferentially recognises F-actin allowed the detection of actin positive structures connecting individual parasites.
source: Labelling parasites with α-actin that preferentially recognises F-actin (Angrisano et al., 2012b) allowed the detection of actin positive structures connecting individual parasites (Figure 6), though the stain appeared more diffuse.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6 and a citation to Angrisano et al., 2012b.

claim: When actin filaments were stabilised by the presence of Jas the α-actin stain becomes more prominent and this was not dependent on the expression of Cb.
source: When actin filaments were stabilised by the presence of Jas (Figure 6) this stain becomes more prominent and this was not dependent on the expression of Cb.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: F-actin is less accessible to exogenously added antibodies after fixation, perhaps due to epitope alterations during fixation or the association of actin binding proteins to filaments.
source: This suggests that F-actin is less accessible to exogenously added antibodies after fixation, perhaps due to epitope alterations during fixation or the association of actin binding proteins to filaments.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed staining patterns.

claim: While actin has never been previously associated with this membranous network in T. gondii, it appears very similar to structures recently described for the related parasite Theileria annulata, which was shown to contain F-actin in a similar configuration.
source: Interestingly, while actin has never been previously associated with this membranous network in T. gondii, it appears very similar to structures recently described for the related parasite Theileria annulata, which was shown to contain F-actin in a similar configuration (Kühni-Boghenbor et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kühni-Boghenbor et al., 2012.

claim: Using a combination of imaging and reverse genetics, F-actin is required for the formation and/or maintenance of the residual body.
source: Using a combination of imaging and reverse genetics, we demonstrate that F-actin is required for the formation and/or maintenance of the residual body.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Parasites lacking actin do not contain a residual body and are disorganized within the PV.
source: Parasites lacking actin do not contain a residual body and are disorganized within the PV.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The residual body and inter-parasite network allow both the free diffusion of cytoplasmic material between parasites, and transport of membrane bound vesicles between parasites.
source: In addition, we show that these extracellular actin-containing structures are required for the transport of material between parasites within a vacuole. The residual body and inter-parasite network allow both the free diffusion of cytoplasmic material between parasites, and transport of membrane bound vesicles between parasites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The organization of F-actin within the parasites and vacuole is highly dynamic throughout the cell cycle.
source: The organization of F-actin within the parasites and vacuole is highly dynamic throughout the cell cycle (Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: In interphase parasites, long inter-parasite contentions extend throughout the PV.
source: In interphase parasites, long inter-parasite contentions extend throughout the PV.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: At the beginning of the replication cycle the F-actin network collapses and is found concentrated in the residual body (or bodies).
source: At the beginning of the replication cycle this network collapses and is found concentrated in the residual body (or bodies).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Within the parasites, F-actin is found concentrated at the IMC of growing daughter cells during elongation.
source: Within the parasites, F-actin is found concentrated at the IMC of growing daughter cells during elongation (Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: As the daughters bud from the mother cell, the inter-parasite connections again extend throughout the PV.
source: As the daughters bud from the mother cell, the inter-parasite connections again extend throughout the PV.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The network collapses in response to calcium ionophore, freeing the parasites and allowing egress.
source: As would be expected, the network also collapses in response to calcium ionophore, freeing the parasites and allowing egress.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: As motile parasites leave the PV, actin appears concentrated at the basal end of parasites.
source: As motile parasites leave the PV, actin appears concentrated at the basal end of parasites (Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The network consists of either short F-actin bundles that are cross-linked via unknown actin-binding proteins or that the presence of actin binding proteins such as formin, profilin, and coronin may coordinate their activities in vivo to produce longer actin filaments than those formed in vitro.
source: While Cb expression allowed us to demonstrate F-actin-containing membranous tubules for the first time, we were unable to assess the length of the individual F-actin filaments using these techniques. We speculate that this network consists of either short F-actin bundles that are cross-linked via unknown actin-binding proteins (based on the formation of short actin filaments in vitro) (Skillman et al., 2011) or that the presence of actin binding proteins such as formin, profilin, and coronin may coordinate their activities in vivo to produce longer actin filaments than those formed in vitro (Skillman et al., 2011; Olshina et al., 2016;Salamun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation, supported by citations to Skillman et al., 2011; Olshina et al., 2016; Salamun et al., 2014.

claim: Highly dynamic actin filaments have been detected within the cytosol of the parasite, and these dynamics are almost completely abolished upon depletion of ADF.
source: While this study focuses on the characterization of the membranous network within the PV, it is worth nothing that highly dynamic actin filaments have been also detected within the cytosol of the parasite, and we show that these dynamics are almost completely abolished upon depletion of ADF in good agreement with previous findings (Haase et al., 2015; Mehta and Sibley, 2011) (Figure 6; Videos 5–7).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Videos 5-7, and citations to Haase et al., 2015; Mehta and Sibley, 2011.

claim: Defining the organization of cytosolic filaments will be critical to further elucidating the role of F-actin both during intracellular processes such as vesicle transport and extracellular processes such as motility and invasion.
source: Defining the organization of cytosolic filaments will be critical to further elucidating the role of F-actin both during intracellular processes such as vesicle transport and extracellular processes such as motility and invasion, where the role of the parasites acto-myosin system is currently readdressed, since parasites devoid of detectable actin remain invasive (Whitelaw et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions, supported by a citation to Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claim: Parasites devoid of detectable actin remain invasive.
source: Defining the organization of cytosolic filaments will be critical to further elucidating the role of F-actin both during intracellular processes such as vesicle transport and extracellular processes such as motility and invasion, where the role of the parasites acto-myosin system is currently readdressed, since parasites devoid of detectable actin remain invasive (Whitelaw et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claim: It appears that host cell membrane dynamics, driven by host cell actin, appears to be modulated by the parasite, enabling invasion in the absence of a functional parasite acto-myosin system.
source: Interestingly, it appears that host cell membrane dynamics, driven by host cell actin, appears to be modulated by the parasite, enabling invasion in the absence of a functional parasite acto-myosin system (Bichet et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bichet et al., 2016.

claim: It is possible that F-actin is organized into distinct, higher order structures, perhaps forming large stable bundles in the tubules while existing as single filaments or small bundles in the cytosol.
source: It is possible that F-actin is organized into distinct, higher order structures, perhaps forming large stable bundles in the tubules while existing as single filaments or small bundles in the cytosol.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed F-actin organization.
